idiom_name: client-created token value + service echo + completion dispatch
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: choose a token representation that is meaningful to the client and opaque to the service (a pointer or reference to completion state, an object reference, or an index into a client-side table); create one before each asynchronous invocation, pass it with the request, and require the service to echo it unchanged with the completion. Keep whatever the token identifies reachable until the completion arrives, dispatch the returned token to the registered completion action in constant time, then release or recycle it. Decide the delivery model explicitly - completion callback pushed by the service, or a completion queue the client pulls from - and fix the multiplicity rule: one token per request that completes once, one token per registration that completes many times, or one token per hop in a chain of services. The four implementation steps are: (1) define ACT representation, (2) pass ACT from client to service, (3) hold ACT at the service in off-stack storage, (4) demultiplex it back to the client on completion.
code_sketch:
token = Token(completion_state)     # created by the client before the call
service.invoke(request, token)     # service holds the opaque token
loop:
    t = completions.next()         # or: callback(t) pushed by the service
    t.state.apply(completion)      # O(1) dispatch, no lookup by request identity
    release(t)
pitfalls: Letting the service interpret the token - or re-deriving it from the response payload - destroys the constant-time property the pattern exists for.
No ownership or expiry rule: tokens whose operations never complete retain the state they reference forever.
Assuming the token stays opaque when it does not: relying on a transport that overwrites token fields (overlapped structures, reused reply slots) instead of reserving room or wrapping the token.
Using pointer tokens across process or address-space boundaries without validation, allowing a malicious or confused peer to forge arbitrary dispatch targets.
Index-based tokens without generation counters: recycling slot indices after operation cleanup can dispatch a stale completion to a reused slot still holding unrelated state.

Wrong move: free or recycle a pointer/index token when submission returns -> a late completion dereferences released or unrelated state -> instead retain it until exactly-once completion or deadline/cancellation, and use generation counters for recycled indices.

Wrong move: let the service interpret or rewrite the token, or reconstruct it from payload fields -> client-specific state leaks into the service contract and dispatch falls back to parsing/search -> instead carry an opaque token unchanged and use an explicit correlation lookup when interpretation is truly required.

Wrong move: reuse a one-shot token for a registration that can notify repeatedly (or free it after the first notification) -> later notifications dispatch into released state or are lost -> instead declare single-use versus multi-use semantics and give each lifecycle an explicit ownership/refcount rule.
sources: Schmidt et al., 'Asynchronous Completion Token - An Object Behavioral Pattern for Efficient Asynchronous Event Handling' (PLoP 1996, also in Pattern Languages of Program Design 3)
